results.description:

In today’s video I’m repotting one of my Adeniums (Desert Roses) and walking you through exactly how I like to do it so you get healthy roots, a happy caudex, and those big knockout blooms.

🌱 My go-to Desert Rose soil mix:
I keep it chunky, airy, and quick-draining so the caudex stays firm and the roots breathe. I usually start with a cactus/succulent base and “Texas-ify” it with extra grit:

Cactus/succulent soil as the base

Add pumice/perlite for drainage

Add pine bark / lava rock / coarse grit for airflow and structure
The goal is a mix that dries out on a reasonable schedule — Adeniums love water, they just hate sitting in it.

results.title: The AMISH Way to Care for Desert Rose in Winter — The Secret to Healthy Growth Next Season
results.description:
👉 Want to learn how to live a simpler, more independent life? Take a deeper look here: https://independentbackyard.com/my-book/#aff=natanaelfernamdes


Sixty-five degrees. That's the temperature where a Desert Rose's growth quietly shuts down, long before any frost warning ever reaches your phone. I am Elias Yoder, and today I'm giving you the exact winter protocol for Adenium obesum — and why treating it like any other cold-hardy succulent is exactly how so many of them are lost every year.

I farm in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. This plant has almost no margin for error around cold, even while it stays remarkably forgiving of nearly everything else. Today's video covers tracking overnight lows instead of daytime highs, deliberately choosing between a real winter rest or genuine active growth, cutting watering down to a fraction of summer levels, checking whether your plant is grafted, never risking an actual freeze, waiting until spring to prune cold damage, keeping even a dormant plant in real light, and reintroducing outdoor sun gradually in spring.

⬇️ Everything covered in this video:
00:00 — The 65-degree threshold nobody warns you about
03:30 — Secret 1: Track nighttime lows, not frost warnings
06:00 — Secret 2: Choose deliberately — rest or active growth
10:00 — Secret 3: Cutting watering down to almost nothing
13:30 — Secret 4: Checking for a graft union
16:00 — Secret 5: Never let it freeze, even briefly
19:00 — Secret 6: Wait until spring to prune cold damage
22:30 — Secret 7: Real light, even for a dormant plant
25:00 — Secret 8: Reintroducing sun gradually in spring

results.title: What To Expect from your Roses in October
results.description:
October is a month of mixed signals in the rose garden. While spring gets all the glory, autumn offers an honest look at how our roses hold up after a full season of growth and weather.

In this video, I walk you through the garden to highlight what is still thriving late in the season, including standouts like Danae and Mel's Heritage that often save their best flush for cool autumn days. Alongside the blooms, we tackle the reality of October garden triage. We take a close look at late-season foliar diseases and whether they warrant action or patience, the perennial debate on whether to prune now or hold off until spring, and how to spot those unruly  canes that need securing before winter storms arrive. Finally, autumn is the ideal time to make cold, calculated decisions: which roses have earned their spot, which might need a better location, and which ones simply deserve to be deleted from the garden altogether.

Grab a warm drink and join me for a realistic walk around the beds as we set our roses up for success before winter sets in.

results.title: STOP! Prune Roses NOW - but avoid these five autumn mistakes!
results.description:
Don't touch those secateurs yet! In this video, we dive into the essential rules of autumn rose care for the Walking Talking Gardeners community. While it might be tempting to give your roses a heavy prune in September, doing it at the wrong time or using the wrong technique can seriously weaken your plants before winter.

We break down the five most common autumn mistakes, from improper tool sterilization to pruning the wrong rose groups. You’ll learn exactly which cuts are safe to make right now—including how to create the perfect "goblet shape" for airflow—and which roses (like Hybrid Teas and Floribundas) should wait until March.

Whether you're tending to climbing roses, rambling roses, or shrub varieties, this guide ensures your garden stays healthy, disease-free, and ready for a spectacular display next spring.

In this video:

How to identify and remove dead, diseased, and crossing branches.
The critical importance of sterilizing your pruning tools.
Understanding the difference between pruning on "old wood" vs. "new wood."
Specific timing and tips for Climbers, Ramblers, Hybrid Teas, and Shrub roses.
How to preserve rose hips for winter wildlife and ornamental value.

results.title: 10 Dollars Tree Garden hacks to keep Your plants Alive all winter long 🔥
results.description:
What if some of the best winter plant protection hacks are hiding at Dollar Tree, in aisles most gardeners walk right past?
 
Every winter, gardeners spend money on frost covers, plant protection supplies, and expensive gardening equipment, yet their plants can still suffer from frozen roots, trapped moisture, and damaging winter winds. But some everyday Dollar Tree items, never intended for gardening, can help tackle these problems for just a few dollars.
 
In this video, we're sharing 10 Dollar Tree garden hacks that can help protect your plants through winter without spending a fortune. From plant saucers and plastic bottles to shower curtain liners, storage bins, burlap, and other unexpected finds, these simple DIY gardening ideas offer practical ways to protect container plants, small garden beds, and delicate seedlings during cold weather.
 
You'll learn how to reduce frost damage, protect potted plant roots from rapid temperature changes, manage excess moisture, and create temporary plant shelters using affordable household items. We'll also cover common winter gardening mistakes that can make even well-intentioned plant protection efforts backfire.
 
And don't miss Hack Number Eight. It's an inexpensive packing material that most people would never think to use in the garden, but it can make a useful difference when protecting potted plants from cold weather.
 
The key is knowing what each hack can and cannot do. Some help during brief cold snaps, while others reduce wind exposure or slow heat loss. None replaces stronger protection when severe freezing weather arrives.
 
Which Dollar Tree garden hack would you try first? Tell me in the comments what gives your plants the most trouble during winter.
